transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I guess… I came in because I keep feeling like I’ve ruined things for everybody. Like I’m a fake in my apprenticeship, and I’m letting my family down, and even the younger apprentices, which probably sounds dramatic because, I mean, at work stuff breaks or goes wrong and other people just fix it and move on.

But I don’t. I keep thinking it’s my fault, like I should’ve known better. And then I’ll remember this one time my uncle told me trades teach you to have a thick skin, and I don’t know, I don’t feel like I have that. I just feel like I’m disappointing everyone.
Have you been feeling down or depressed most days?

I’m not sure if I’d say “most days,” exactly. I mean, I feel down a lot, but then I also kind of get distracted by work stuff, like if we’re on a job and someone’s asking me to grab fittings or check measurements, I can just focus on that for a while. But when it’s quiet, yeah, it sort of comes back. I don’t know if that counts as depressed most days or just… me not handling things great.
Do you often avoid speaking up or getting involved because you’re afraid people will judge or reject you?

I don’t know… maybe sometimes? Like at work I’ll hesitate before saying something because I don’t want to sound stupid, especially if the journeymen are talking fast and I’m still trying to catch up. But I’m not sure if that’s “rejection” exactly.

It’s more like… I’ll overthink it, and then the moment passes. Like there was this time with a pipe threader where I thought something was off, but then I started wondering if I was just being annoying, and then someone else noticed it anyway. So I guess I do hold back sometimes, but I don’t know if it’s because I’m afraid people will judge me or just because I don’t trust myself.
Did these feelings start after a particular stressful event or change in your life?

Yeah, I think it started after I took on this sustainable plumbing certification, on top of my apprenticeship. It was supposed to be a good thing, like make me more useful or whatever, and I do like learning that stuff—water-saving systems and all that—but it kind of added this whole extra layer.

I guess this has been going on about five months now. Around when I started that, things just started feeling heavier, like I couldn’t keep up as well.
If the certification were taken off your plate tomorrow, do you think you’d mostly go back to feeling like yourself?

Maybe? I mean, it would probably help, because that certification is like this constant thing in the back of my head. But I don’t think it would just disappear overnight.

Honestly, the low stretch has been around longer than that… like maybe nine months? It just got harder to cover up once school and work started slipping. Before, I could kind of act like I was just tired or busy, you know? But then missing things or falling behind made it more obvious.
Have you been enjoying things less than you usually do?

Yeah… I think so. It’s kind of weird because it’s not like I hate those things now, I just don’t really… reach for them.

Like my sketchbook will be sitting right there and I’ll just walk past it. And volleyball—I used to really like going, even if I wasn’t that good, because it got me out of my head. Now I’ll skip it and barely even feel bad about it. Same with the volunteer group chat, they’ll text about stuff and I just ignore it, which is not really like me.

Those used to be the things that made me feel like myself, I guess. Lately they just feel kind of far away.
Have there been at least two weeks when you felt down or cut off from things you usually enjoy nearly every day?

Yeah… definitely more than two weeks. It’s been kind of this long stretch, like maybe around nine months where I’ve felt pretty down and disconnected from stuff most days.

I mean, it wasn’t always dramatic or anything. Sometimes I’d tell myself I was just busy, or tired, or that everyone gets like that. But once school and work started slipping, it was harder to hide it or pretend it was nothing.
Have you noticed a change in your sleep?

Yeah, my sleep’s been kind of all over the place.

For a while I was only getting like three or four hours and somehow still showing up to the job or class really wired, like I’d had way too much coffee even when I hadn’t. Which, honestly, on a job site people just think you’re being productive or whatever, so it didn’t seem that strange at first.

But lately it’s more like… I either can’t fall asleep, or I wake up before my alarm and feel like I didn’t actually rest at all. Like I was technically in bed, but it doesn’t feel like it counted.
During that time when you were sleeping only three or four hours, did you feel unusually energized or revved up?

Yeah. Revved up is probably the right word.

It was like I had this charge in my body that wouldn’t shut off. I’d do a whole day working on pipes, and instead of coming home and crashing like a normal person, I’d go to evening class, then come back and reorganize all my tools, clean my apartment, and sometimes start drawing out systems or layouts like it was suddenly the most important thing.

And I mean, my tool bag does get messy, so part of me was like, “Well, this is useful,” but it was more than that. I just couldn’t really sit down.
When you were only sleeping three or four hours, did you still feel rested?

Yeah, weirdly, I did. Or at least I thought I did.

Like, I’d only sleep three or four hours and then still get up and go to the job site, then class, and I’d feel wired instead of tired. It didn’t feel like normal rested exactly, more like my body was just… running anyway.

Now it’s different, though. Lately I either can’t fall asleep, or I wake up before my alarm and feel like I didn’t actually sleep at all.
During that wired period, were you talking more than usual?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, I didn’t notice it as much at first, because in class we’re always kind of talking through problems or at the shop people are explaining stuff anyway.

But I’d start explaining some idea and then just keep going. Like I’d be talking about a layout or how something could be done, and then I’d realize I was talking over somebody, or they were trying to get back to work and I was still going, barely stopping to breathe.

It’s embarrassing, honestly, because at the time I felt like I was just being clear or helpful, but looking back, yeah, it was more than usual.
About how many days in a row did that wired period last?

It’s kind of hard to separate it into, like, one clean stretch of days. The whole pattern’s been going on for about five months, I guess—since I started the sustainable plumbing certification on top of my apprenticeship.

That’s when everything kind of ramped up. I thought I was just motivated because it was a good opportunity, and the instructors were talking about greywater systems and efficiency stuff, which is actually pretty interesting, but… yeah, it’s been months, not just a couple days.
During that wired period, did you feel unusually confident in yourself or your abilities?

Yeah… I did. At the time it didn’t feel like “overconfident,” it felt like I was just finally seeing what everyone else was missing.

Like, I honestly thought I could design systems better than the instructors or the senior guys on site. I’d be sitting there thinking, if people would just listen to me, we could change how every building in Miami handles water. Which sounds… a lot, saying it now.

I got really caught up in that whole idea, like greywater and reuse and all that, and I was sure I had it figured out better than people who’ve been doing this way longer than me.
During that wired period, did you do anything that got you into trouble or was clearly unusual for you?

Yeah… I don’t know if I’d say “trouble” like serious trouble, but I definitely did stuff that wasn’t normal for me.

I signed myself up to help a bunch of classmates with their projects, and then I was volunteering for extra design sketches too, like anytime someone mentioned an idea I’d be like, “Oh, I can draw that up.” And I started messaging old contacts about possible side projects, even people I hadn’t talked to in a while.

At the time it felt productive, like I was networking or whatever, but then I’d look at my week and it was like… there was no way the hours actually fit. Part of me knew that, but I kept saying yes anyway.
During that wired period, did other people notice you were acting differently than usual?

Yeah, people noticed. In class especially, or at the shop, I’d start explaining some idea I had and then I’d just… keep going. Like way past what the question needed.

I could see people kind of trying to jump in, or the instructor trying to move on, or the guys needing to get back to work, and I’d still be talking over them, barely stopping to breathe. And sometimes it was about the project, but then I’d end up on, like, how the whole system should be redesigned, or this thing I saw in a building downtown, and I’d realize later nobody had asked for all that.

And sometimes it was about the project, but then I’d end up on, like, how the whole system should be redesigned, or this thing I saw in a building downtown, and I’d realize later nobody had asked for all that.

This makes bipolar II disorder the leading diagnosis and rules against F43.2 and F41.1 as primary explanations; depressive episode remains as part of bipolar spectrum, so F32.1 is retained as a differential/state description.
